title: 手把手教你用Claude Code和Obsidian搭建本地AI知识库！
text:
Even though Claude Code has 'Code' in its name,
it's not just an AI tool for programming.
Its best use for regular folks
is actually building a local AI knowledge base.
Because not everyone needs to code,
but most people have a need
to organize their notes and materials.
A while back, AI guru Karpathy posted on GitHub
a methodology he created
for setting up a local AI knowledge base.
After its release, it quickly blew up within the AI community,
both here and abroad.
In this video,
I'll be providing a practical guide
based on this methodology.
I'll walk you through, step by step,
how to set up an AI knowledge base system
on your own computer,
just like Karpathy's.
I'll also show you
how to use Claude Code
to manage your knowledge base
in a completely offline environment,
with no internet connection.
So please, while you're adding this to your favorites,
give it a like to show your support,
and if you could follow me, that'd be even better!
Oh, by the way, I've also put together a detailed, document
version of this video—check the comments section
if you need it.
First, let's install all the software
we need to set up a local AI knowledge base.
So, the software we'll need for this is as follows:
Claude Code, Obsidian, LM Studio,
and the Obsidian Web Clipper browser extension.
As for installing Claude Code,
I won't go into detail
here; you can check out the official installation methods
they provide.
Whether you're on Windows or Mac,
it's basically just a one line command—super simple.
Obsidian is a super popular Markdown
note taking app right now.
Its biggest feature is that
all note files are stored locally,
making it perfect for housing a local knowledge base.
Just head over to the official site
to download and install it—it's super straightforward.
Also, if you're dealing with sensitive
personal or company data,
you'll probably need a knowledge base
that's completely offline
and has no internet connection.
For that, you'll need to install LM Studio.
What it does is let you download various open source models
and run them on your local computer for Claude Code to use.
We'll get into how to use it later on.
Lastly, we'll also be using a browser plugin from Obsidian
called the Obsidian Web Clipper.
Its purpose is to let us easily import webpage content
into Obsidian
with just one click—just head over to the Chrome or Edge
browser plugin store
and install it.
Now that we've covered the software,
let's briefly talk about the hardware.
If the data you're managing
doesn't contain any sensitive information,
then the system we're building
this time has no special requirements
for your computer—any laptop or desktop will do.
But if you often need to organize
personal or company sensitive data
and require a completely offline environment,
then there are some specific requirements
for your computer's specs.
That's because a purely offline environment
requires running large models locally,
which needs a good amount of RAM and GPU VRAM to load them.
For instance, you'll want at least thirty two
gigabytes of RAM,
and ideally, sixteen gigabytes or more of VRAM.
Alternatively, you can get a machine with Unified Memory .
For example, this ASUS ProArt PX thirteen laptop
I have right here
is powered by an AMD Ryzen AI Max
x+ three hundred and ninety five processor.
Unlike traditional laptops, it uses Unified Memory ,
which means the CPU, GPU, and NPU
all share the same physical memory
and a unified address Space.
This eliminates the need to copy data
between system memory and VRAM,
drastically reducing data interaction latency.
Plus, it supports AMD's Variable Memory technology,
which lets you customize
how memory is allocated right from the driver.
For example, this machine has a total of sixty four
gigabytes of Unified Memory .
I set forty eight gigabytes of that as dedicated VRAM,
leaving the remaining sixteen gigabytes
for the system to run normally.
This way, even running a thirty B model
locally will be more than enough.
Okay,
Next up, let's talk about
how to deploy a large language model locally.
We've just downloaded LM Studio,
and you can search directly within it
for any open source models you want to download,
like Qwen or DeepSeek, and so on.
But with so many models out there, how do we choose?
A lot of people just look at the parameter count.
Actually, when picking a model,
you need to focus on two metrics:
first, the quantized model file size,
and second, the KV Cache usage for your target context length.
To get the model to run smoothly,
this formula has to hold true:
the model file size
plus the KV Cache usage plus runtime overhead
must be less than your available VRAM.
For example, a thirty B Q four quantized model
has a file size of about eighteen to twenty gigs.
But if you need it to process
a one hundred and twenty eight K context,
its KV Cache plus the runtime VRAM overhead ...
that can easily chew up another ten plus gigs,
bringing the total to at least thirty gigs of available VRAM
just to get it running properly.
And that's why it's so hard to do this
on a regular thin and light laptop.
In fact, forget about thin and light
laptops—even a top spec rig
with a fifty ninety GPU
usually only has twenty four gigs of VRAM.
Faced with this kind of demand
that can easily eat up thirty gigabytes of VRAM,
it has to resort to memory offload—basically,
borrowing system RAM to force it to run.
But once the VRAM can't handle it
and has to pull data from elsewhere,
the token generation speed will plummet.
But this ASUS ProArt PX thirteen,
with its forty eight gigabytes of available VRAM,
can not only fit the thirty B model entirely,
but also fully run its two hundred K context window
at the same time.
Only when both of these conditions are met
do you have a setup
that can truly handle large scale knowledge bases.
I remember back when I ran these large models
on my old machine,
the CPU and GPU would constantly max out and go red hot,
spitting out tokens like squeezing toothpaste,
and it would lag all the time.
But this laptop, powered by an AMD Ryzen processor,
not only handles the hardware load with ease,
The speed at which it spits out tokens
is visibly silky smooth,
with zero lag—it's a night and day difference in experience.
So, with this hardware as a foundation,
I went straight for the Qwen thirty B Q four
quantized version—just click download in LM Studio
and you're good to go.
Once it's downloaded,
switch over to the 'Developer' tab on the left
and flip on the 'Server' toggle.
LM Studio then exposes the local model as an API endpoint,
typically at HTTP colon slash slash
localhost:twelve thirty four.
Remember this address, as we'll need it for the next step.
Once the local model is up and running,
the next step is to connect Claude Code to it.
The process is also super simple.
Just find the `.claude` folder in your system's user directory
and open up the `settings.json` file inside.
Here, we need to change three things.
First, the API endpoint—just fill in that LM Studio address
we just had.
Next up is the auth token—just type in some random letters
to fill the spot.
Lastly, for the three model fields below,
change them all to the model ID you just downloaded.
Once that's done, save the file,
reopen your terminal, type 'claude',
and as long as the interface pops up normally,
it means the connection was successful.
And you don't need to memorize all this code.
I've put the complete configuration template in the docs,
so you can just copy, paste, and tweak it as needed.
Now, let's cover the final piece of the knowledge base:
an Obsidian plugin called Claudian.
Since it hasn't been published
on the official Obsidian Plugin
Market yet,
So, you'll need to install the BRAT plugin,
which is a utility
specifically for installing third party beta plugins.
In BRAT, just enter the open source project address
for Claude,
and it'll automatically install it for you.
Lastly, don't forget to head back to the plugin list
and enable Claudian.
Once installed, what it does is actually quite intuitive:
it embeds Claude Code right into Obsidian's sidebar,
turning your Obsidian
note vault into Claude Code's working directory.
It can directly read files, write files,
search, and even execute tasks right within it.
This perfectly recreates the workflow
that Karpathy described.
On the left, you have your knowledge base;
on the right, the Claude Code assistant.
The LLM is modifying your files,
and you can watch the results in real time
right alongside it.
Alright, with that, all the environment setup is complete.
Now, let's officially start
the knowledge base building process.
First, let's create an empty vault in Obsidian,
and then just drop the original Andrej Karpathy LLM
Wiki article
right into it.
Then, in Claudian, give Claude Code
this command: 'Please do a deep read of this article
and initialize my knowledge base
based on the methodology within it.'
And now for the magic moment—it'll automatically
create these core directories
for you.
The 'raw' folder—basically your inbox—where you'll store
all your unprocessed, raw materials.
The VK folder—this is the LLM's dedicated domain,
where all the generated and categorized pages live.
index.md.
md is the directory outline for the entire vk folder,
and log.md ...
log.md is an append only operation log.
And what's even cooler
is that it automatically extracts the essence of articles
and generates a CLAUDE.md file.
This is like it wrote itself an employee handbook,
which strictly lays out the directory structure,
tagging conventions, and rules for bidirectional links.
From now on,
whenever new data is tossed in, it'll
dutifully follow the rules
in this manual
to get to work.
Once this skeleton is built,
we can start putting stuff inside.
Kaspersky believes that traditional knowledge bases
are hard to stick with
because humans hate tedious bookkeeping tasks
like tagging and indexing.
So now, we just focus on feeding it data
and let the AI handle the bookkeeping.
Hey everyone.
Open your browser,
find an article you want to save,
and click on the Obsidian Web Clipper icon.
The article is saved as Markdown in the 'raw' folder—clean,
plain text, and completely local.
Then, within Claudian, we tell Claude Code
that a new article has been added to 'raw'—please process it.
Note: in Karpathy's theory,
this isn't called 'reading,' it's called 'compiling.'
The AI will act like a compiler,
turning the raw source materials into structured knowledge
within the wiki.
It will distill the core of the articles
to generate summary pages,
and extract the key concepts within them
into separate entity pages.
and cross reference them using Obsidian's
unique bidirectional
links.
Finally, it updates the index directory
and writes the log file.
This seamless, hands free series of actions
is the system's core 'Ingest' and compilation process.
Now that the data's in,
let's try querying it—this is where this whole setup
absolutely blows
traditional RAG out of the water.
So, in the chat box, we'll ask it:
what's the core argument of this article?
And how does it relate to the content
already in the knowledge base?
Now, watch what Claude Code does:
it first opens the index to browse the directory,
pinpointing those highly relevant wiki pages
and loading them one by one.
Finally, it delivers a high quality answer
synthesized from your personal database,
meticulously citing which original articles it drew from.
More importantly,
traditional RAG forgets everything after the chat,
so next time,
you have to start the retrieval process all over again.
But with this system,
the knowledge compounds—your high quality
answer itself gets saved back into the wiki
as a new analysis report.
This means that with every question you ask,
every interaction you have,
this knowledge base grows automatically,
like a living organism,
getting smarter and smarter.
Alright, that's all for today.
We've successfully implemented
Andrej Karpathy's LLM Wiki methodology
using Claude Code,
Obsidian, and LM Studio—let's do a quick recap.
The core of it boils down to three things:
first, write up the CLAUDE.md file,
basically, setting the rules like in an employee handbook;
and second, dumping
all the raw materials you've gathered into the 'raw' folder.
And finally, just sit back
and watch your local AI compile that knowledge into a wiki
for you.
And since we're talking about
advanced local AI agent setups today,
I've got some good news to share with you all.
AMD recently launched the Ryzen AI Agent
Innovation Application Contest.
So if you're interested in this kind of AI native workflow,
or have even cooler ideas and use cases of your own,
I highly recommend
giving it a shot—you might just snag a grand prize!
I'll drop the sign up link in the comments and description.
And as for what's been with us
for this whole run today—this local LLM powerhouse—it's
this ASUS ProArt PX thirteen right here.
Don't let its sleek, slim appearance
fool you—it's super convenient
for daily carry—but underneath,
it's a true AI performance beast.
If you have an in depth need for local large language models,
I highly recommend checking out its top spec version
with one hundred and twenty eight
gigabytes of Unified Memory ,
which can allocate a ridiculously huge VRAM pool.
Running hundred billion parameter models
is a breeze—definitely one of the most
elegant and portable solutions
for running large local models right now.
If this video was helpful,
don't forget to like, follow, and show some support!
I'm Ah Zhong,
see you next time!

# 本地 AI 知识库系统图谱

## 系统组件概览
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Claude Code"] -->|使用 API| B["LM Studio"]
    A -->|通过 Claudian 插件集成| E["Claudian 插件"]
    B -->|暴露本地 LLM API| H["本地 LLM API"]
    H -->|运行于| G["硬件 (CPU/GPU/VRAM)"]
    D["Obsidian Web Clipper"] -->|导入网页内容| C["Obsidian"]
    C -->|存储 Vault| I["知识库 (Vault)"]
    E -->|嵌入| A
    F["BRAT 插件"] -->|安装| E
    A -->|读写文件| I
```

## 硬件与模型选择要求
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    H1["是否处理敏感数据？"] --> H2["需要完全离线环境"]
    H2 --> H3["模型文件大小"]
    H2 --> H4["KV Cache 使用量"]
    H3 --> H5["可用 VRAM"]
    H4 --> H5
    H5 --> H6["RAM ≥ 32 GB"]
    H5 --> H7["VRAM ≥ 16 GB 或统一内存"]
    H6 & H7 --> H8["模型能否装入内存？"]
    H8 --> H9["选择合适模型"]
    H9 --> H10["示例：ASUS ProArt PX13（48 GB VRAM）"]
```

## 环境搭建工作流
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S1["安装 Claude Code"] --> S5["配置 LM Studio 服务器"]
    S2["安装 Obsidian"] --> S9["创建 Obsidian Vault"]
    S3["安装 LM Studio"] --> S5
    S4["安装 Obsidian Web Clipper"] --> S9
    S5 --> S6["编辑 .claude/settings.json"]
    S6 --> S7["设置 API 地址、Token、模型 ID"]
    S7 --> S10["启动 Claude Code"]
    S8["安装 BRAT 与 Claudian"] --> S9
    S9 --> S10
```

## 内容摄取与编译流程
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    I1["使用 Web Clipper 添加文章"] --> I2["保存至 raw 文件夹"]
    I2 --> I3["在 Claudian 中发出编译指令"]
    I3 --> I4["LLM 读取 raw 内容"]
    I4 --> I5["生成 VK 页面（结构化知识）"]
    I5 --> I6["更新 index.md 与 log.md"]
    I5 --> I7["生成 CLAUDE.md（手册）"]
    I5 --> I8["创建双向链接"]
    I8 --> I6
```

## 查询、回答与知识库自增长
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q1["用户提问"] --> Q2["Claude Code 检索 index"]
    Q2 --> Q3["加载相关页面"]
    Q3 --> Q4["生成高质量答案"]
    Q4 --> Q5["引用原始文章"]
    Q5 --> Q6["写入分析报告到 Wiki"]
    Q6 --> Q7["知识库自动扩展"]
```
